label: New class or club

what_happens.title: What happens at a new class
goals: A class has a warm-up, learning and a goodbye
The teacher shows first, then everyone tries
what_happens.parentSkill: Watch a short video of the activity together and name the first move or note.

who_is_there.title: Who is at the class
goals: The teacher or coach shows and helps
Some kids have done it before
who_is_there.parentSkill: Arrive a few minutes early so your child can meet the teacher before the room gets busy.

what_i_do.title: What I do in the class
what_i_do.parentSkill: Praise effort: "You kept trying that hard part."

if_scared.title: If it feels hard
goals: Feeling clumsy or shy is normal
Calm tools: breathing, trying a smaller step, a break
if_scared.parentSkill: Name the feeling and shrink the step: 'It feels hard. Let's try just the first part.'

rehearsal.title: Let's practise the first class
goals: Try one basic move or note at home
rehearsal.parentSkill: Learn one beginner move or note together from a video and laugh at your own attempts.

steps: Pack the bag with the right clothes or instrument
Arrive and find the room or the hall
Meet the teacher or coach and say hello
Watch the teacher show the first moves or notes
Try it with the group, step by step
Finish, say goodbye and tell what was fun
sensory: a big hall or a studio with mirrors
music, a drum or an instrument sound
a new uniform, leotard or belt
a squeaky floor or soft mats
honestyNotes: Learning a new skill feels awkward at first and children may feel clumsy or behind; never promise it will be easy. It is okay not to like a class, but encourage trying a few times before deciding. Let the parent fill in which class it is.

questionButtons.text: What if I am not good at it?
fallbackAnswer: Everyone starts as a beginner, even the teacher once did.
You get a little better each class.
A teacher or coach whose job is showing kids how to do it.
They will say hello and help you.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you if they watch, wait outside or come back at the end.
They will be there when class finishes.
Maybe not at first, and that is okay.
You can say hello, and friends grow over the weeks.
[[GROWNUP]] will find out and pack the right clothes with you.
Some classes have a uniform, a leotard or a belt.
Some activities can make muscles tired or a bit sore after.
Warm-ups help, and you can tell the teacher if something hurts.

questionButtons.text: What if I don't like it?
fallbackAnswer: It is okay to not like it at first. Let's try a few times.
Then we can talk about it together.
Music, drums or lots of kids can be loud.
You can take a quiet break or ask the teacher.
Every class has a few rules to keep everyone safe.
The teacher will tell you, and you can ask.

questionButtons.text: Can I quit if it is boring?
fallbackAnswer: We can talk about it after a few classes.
Sometimes things get more fun once you learn the basics.

techniques.label: Watching first
techniques.how: Watch for a few minutes before joining in.

techniques.label: Arriving early
techniques.how: Arrive early to meet the teacher in a quiet room.

techniques.label: Learning one move
techniques.how: Learn one basic move or note at home first.

techniques.label: Asking to see it again
techniques.how: Practise: can you show me again, please?

techniques.label: Try it four times
techniques.how: Agree to try four classes before deciding.

techniques.label: Praising effort
techniques.how: Praise trying hard, not being good.

techniques.label: A quiet break
techniques.how: Take a short break if it feels like too much.

techniques.label: A goodbye wave
techniques.how: Agree a wave through the window if you wait outside.

ritual: Pack my bag and say hello

pain: If your muscles feel tired, take a break and drink water.
Tell the teacher if something hurts.
body: Your body is learning something new.
sensory: The music is loud. You can take a quiet break.
The room is big at first and then feels normal.
strangers: The teacher's job is to help beginners.
You can say, hi, I'm new.
separation: I will be there at the end.
safety: The class rules keep everyone safe.
Ask when something is not clear.
love: I'm proud of you for trying something new.
I love you whether you love the class or not.

sentences.text: Soon [[CHILD]] will go to a new class or club.
It might be dance, karate, music, art, gymnastics or something else.
First [[CHILD]] changes into the right clothes or gets the instrument ready.
Then the class says hello and warms up.
[[CHILD]] can watch the teacher closely, then try.
Before bed, here is a story about a little penguin called Pim.
Pim wanted to learn to dance.
So Pim went to the Ice Hall dance class.
First Pim put on little red dancing shoes.
Then the class waddled in a circle to warm up.
Next the teacher, a graceful swan, showed a spin.
Watch my feet, said the swan, slowly, slowly.
After that, the penguins tried.
Pim spun, wobbled and plopped onto a soft mat.
Everyone giggled, and Pim giggled too.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
Next the teacher shows something new, slowly.
After that, everyone tries it, step by step.
There is a water break in the middle.
Last, the class says goodbye until next time.
[[CHILD]] can watch the teacher closely, then try.
Step by step, it all gets a little easier.

Most activities build skills in layers: basics first, then combinations, then performances or grades.
Beginner classes are designed for people who know nothing yet.
Progress often feels slow for a few weeks and then suddenly clicks.
Many clubs have levels, belts or certificates that mark progress.
[[CHILD]] can ask the teacher what the first goal is.
Instructors are usually trained in teaching kids and keeping them safe in the activity.
Mixed-level classes mean there are role models to watch.
Asking an experienced kid for a tip is a good way to start a friendship.
Some classes ask parents to wait outside so kids can focus.
[[CHILD]] can ask a classmate how long they have been coming.
Learning a physical or musical skill uses muscle memory, which builds through repetition, not just understanding.
Breaking a skill into tiny steps makes it easier to master.
Feeling awkward is a sign the brain is learning something new.
Most teachers love questions because they show attention.
[[CHILD]] can practise one small thing for five minutes at home between classes.
Comparing yourself to someone with two years of practice is not a fair comparison.
Embarrassment fades fast because others are focused on their own moves.
Committing to a set number of classes, like four, before deciding gives the skill time to grow.
Sometimes a class really is not a good fit, and that is useful to know.
[[CHILD]] can track one small improvement after each class.
Knowing a single basic move or rule before class makes the first lesson less overwhelming.
Checking the location, the entrance and what to wear removes small worries.
Arriving early gives time to meet the teacher.
A short practice plan, like five minutes three times a week, is better than one long session.
[[CHILD]] can make a progress chart for the first month.
